maintopic: REPORT ON CANADIAN MISSION TO UNITED KINGDOM

speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
maintopic: REPORT ON CANADIAN MISSION TO UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thought I might take a few minutes to give a brief, interim report on the Canadian trade mission which is now in the city of Glasgow. I returned this morning from Glasgow, and I thought perhaps the house would like to know how the mission is getting on. Hon. members will recall that it left Canada on November 21 with the approval of all parties in the house; that it consisted of over 50 people representing all provinces and about 20 of the major industries in this country, and representatives from the fishing industry, agriculture and labour.
The mission arrived safely by T.C.A. on November 22 and was received in the customary friendly way by the people of the United Kingdom. We were met at the airport by the secretary of state for commonwealth affairs, the president of the board of trade, our own high commissioner, Hon. George Drew, and Sir William Rootes, who is chairman of the dollar exports council. Mr. Drew and I, along with Sir David Eccles and Lord Home, then paid a visit to Prime Minister Harold Macmillan, who spent half an hour with us discussing the purpose of the mission and wishing us well on our tour of the United Kingdom.
The reception by the people of the British isles, according to members of the British press, has surpassed anything within recent years except perhaps a visit from a member 96698-112
of some royal family. There has been an intense interest in the mission throughout the United Kingdom.
The press conference on the day we arrived had representatives from almost every newspaper in the United Kingdom. I counted more members of the press at the conference than there were members of the Canadian trade mission, and some of our reporters estimated there were 100 members of the press present on that occasion. This gives you an idea of the interest which was created in the mission before it set foot in England. The response since has been tremendous. Every day, on TV or radio or in the press, word has been carried throughout the British isles concerning the trade mission. The London newspapers, cramped though they are for space, have given some attention to the mission, and the newspapers in the provinces have in their turn given very good attention to the trade mission.
When we arrived in Glasgow just two days ago we were of course met at the station by a pipe band and 500 people who arrived to bid the Canadians welcome. They were not invited particularly, but they knew about the mission through the publicity the British press had given to it. The preparations made in the United Kingdom for the mission were elaborate and very well done indeed. The board of trade, under Sir David Eccles and his officials, operated closely with Sir William Rootes of the dollar exports council and with our own high commissioner and his officials at Canada House in the preparation of every detail for this mission, the largest and most representative to reach the shores of England.
The interest of the British businessmen in the mission has surpassed all expectations, either on our part or the part of the people in the United Kingdom. The mission is visiting quite a number of industrial plants in England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland to see for themselves the progress of British industry. So much interest has been created in this visit that 700 British firms, in addition to the ones we are visiting, have written to the board of trade, the dollar exports council or Canada House asking for an opportunity to meet the members of the mission. This was totally unexpected, but we have made provision for that because within ten days' time the members of the mission will be in London for a three-day stay and offices have been provided for the purpose of seeing that the British businessmen who are

Trade Mission to United Kingdom, interested may meet face to face with our Canadian representatives. This will give you some idea of the interest that has been aroused in the United Kingdom as a result of this visit.
Before I left we had seen a number of industrial plants, and all of us were impressed by the progress that has been made. It appears that a full recovery has been achieved in England from the war damage and from the early post-war years. The factories are coming into full production. They are efficient and well managed. A considerable amount of automation has been introduced into the factories. The British workingman is working efficiently and rapidly. The housekeeping arrangement in the factory was a matter of considerable comment by experienced members of our mission. All told, we were surprised and delighted to see how well advanced British industry is. We were similarly delighted and pleased to see the great interest that the British people have in Canada.
We announced that we had arrived to fulfil two main purposes: first, to investigate for ourselves and see the progress of British industry and its productivity; and second, to inform British businessmen of the great opportunities awaiting them in Canada. We pointed out that our imports into Canada reached the total of $5,700 million per year; that Britain prior to the second world war enjoyed an 18 per cent share of imports into Canada; that such share had now dropped down to about 8J. per cent to 9 per cent; and that in our opinion there was an opportunity at this stage for British businessmen to reenter the Canadian field and to bring to our shores some of the products which they can so skilfully make because they have the skill and the ingenuity.
We noted with a great deal of interest their very fine apprenticeship system to train their mechanics and their technical experts. We also noted their courses for training their managerial staff. We saw with our own eyes the amenities that are provided for people working in the plants in the way of up to date canteens, recreational facilities and medical and hospital facilities. Along with Sir William Rootes, Mr. Schollie, our labour representative, and Mr. James Duncan, I had the pleasure of meeting with a group in one of the factories, of the shop stewards and others who were selected to represent the views of those who are engaged in the work in the factories. We exchanged opinions and told them about our mission, and they gave us some of their views with regard to what can be accomplished by British industry.
All told, the mission has been a great success. It has carried the name of Canada

to the British isles in a way that name has not been carried since the end of the war. The warm feeling of the people in the United Kingdom for Canada cannot be fully expressed by me here this afternoon. It must be experienced to be completely appreciated.
Canada stands very high in the opinion of the United Kingdom. Among the members of our mission and the British people we met over there in conference after conference, there was general agreement that this is a very appropriate time for Canada and the United Kingdom to draw more closely together, not only in trade but in all other ways.

speakeroldname: Hon. D. S. Harkness (Minister of Agriculture):
maintopic: BEEF CATTLE-STATEMENT ON EXPORTS TO THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a statement in connection with exports of beef cattle from Canada to the United States, as this is a matter of considerable concern and uncertainty at the moment.
During the past few days there have been conflicting reports as to the status of the last

quarterly quota on cattle weighing over 700 pounds entering the United States, with news reports to the effect that United States customs were collecting additional duty on cattle over 700 pounds. The latest information available is that, as of November 23, 93,200 head of cattle over 700 pounds from all countries have entered the United States during the last quarter of the year, which would leave a balance of 26,800 head to fill the quota of 120,000 head permitted under the quarterly global quota. Actual exports of cattle weighing over 700 pounds from Canada to the United States for the last quarter are not available, but the exports approximate
79.000,	with Mexican imports approximating
14.000.
We are advised that United States customs officers have not been instructed to and are not as yet collecting extra duty, but they have been instructed to date stamp all invoices in view of the fact that the quarterly quota is approaching completion.
Notwithstanding the fact that United States customs collectors are not actually as yet collecting extra duty, there is reason to believe that certain United States customs brokers handling shipments of Canadian cattle are collecting extra duty as a protection to themselves. This is probably the basis for the news reports that additional duty is being collected. It is customary for the United States customs officers to start collecting duty when the cattle quota for those over 700 pounds is approaching completion. Any duty collected by either the United States customs officers or brokers on cattle which eventually prove to be within the quota will be refunded.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. MacLean (Minister of Fisheries):
maintopic: FURTHER STATEMENT AS TO IMPORTS FROM JAPAN
speechtext:
On Friday last, November 29, the hon. member for New Westminster asked if I had received a letter from the united fishermen and allied workers' union concerning the importation of Japanese canned salmon. I replied at that time that I had, but to clarify the situation I think I should add to the brief answer I gave at that time.
The 1956 and 1957 salmon catches in British Columbia failed to produce sufficient supplies of certain species of salmon to fill the requirements of the Canadian market. The Canadian consumption of canned sock-eye salmon has been running in the vicinity of 300,000 cases annually. In the sockeye season just ended only about 225,000 cases were packed, as compared with the average of 440,000 cases for the preceding five years.
The small catches in 1956 and 1957 were due principally to the failure of the runs of salmon to a number of the major producing areas, particularly in the north. Prior to the 1956 salmon fishing season in British Columbia it was known that one of the major river systems would not be a large producer. Hence in the fall of 1955 it was anticipated that there would be a shortage of canned Canadian sockeye salmon from the 1956 season.
In anticipation of the short packs of sockeye and pink salmon in 1956 and the short pack in 1957 of sockeye, the industry considered

Inquiries of the Ministry that it was most desirable to share the available Canadian canned salmon pack with buyers in the United Kingdom, which market has been a traditional one for Canadian canned salmon and is an important one to retain. The maintenance of the British market for Canadian canned salmon is important for both the fishermen and the operating companies of British Columbia.
Because of this situation it was necessary for the processing companies to supplement the stocks of canned salmon for the Canadian market by importing some species of canned salmon from Japan. This has resulted in the appearance of Japanese canned salmon in Canadian food stores, and has no doubt puzzled some consumers who have always looked upon canned salmon as an exclusively Canadian product. In view of the short supplies in 1956 and 1957 of some species of Canadian canned salmon, chiefly sockeye, it would seem to be good business to make available to the consumer a continuous supply of canned salmon, and this was done by importing high quality canned salmon from the only available source of supply, Japan.
When it was foreseen that there would be a short supply of Canadian canned salmon in the 1956 pack year, processing companies consulted with and advised the united fishermen and allied workers' union of their intention to bring in some supplies of the canned product from Japan. The union at that time concurred in the proposal of the companies. Approximately 165,000 cases of sockeye salmon were imported from Japan in 1956, and in the same year about 40,000 cases of pinks and approximately 40,000 cases of cohoe. The figures I have quoted are for full cases of 48 pounds.
In view of the small Canadian pack of sockeye salmon in 1957 it is understood the processing companies expect to import from Japan, but only sufficient quantities of canned sockeye salmon which will meet the requirements of the domestic market until the new Canadian pack of 1958 is available. The canned salmon industry of British Columbia is confident that the current shortage of sockeye salmon is only temporary, and that in 1958 ample supplies of Canadian production will again be available.
In the meantime, however, it is felt to be important that the market demand for sockeye salmon be satisfied, and that the competitive position of sockeye salmon with other foods be protected. I consider it fortunate that this supply shortage of canned salmon can be filled from Japan, an important buyer of such Canadian products as wheat, pulp, iron ore and other raw materials. It is fortunate too that the temporary shortage of Canadian

canned salmon is chiefly confined to the sockeye species. The industry feels that sufficient supplies of Canadian produced cohoe, pinks and chums will be available to the Canadian consumer.
It is important to emphasize that all canned salmon entering Canada must be inspected for quality and high standard under the regulations for the inspection of canned salmon of the Canadian Meat and Canned Foods Act. The same rigid inspection is given to imported canned salmon as to the Canadian product. This inspection is carried out by the inspection service of the Department of Fisheries at its Vancouver laboratory.
In addition to the Canadian government inspection regulations, I am informed that the major importing companies send their own personnel to Japan to inspect very thoroughly all parcels of Japanese canned salmon which they expect to purchase. Thus it can be said that the Japanese canned salmon product undergoes very careful and thorough examination for quality, first by the purchasing companies and then by the Department of Fisheries, before the product is offered for sale in Canada.
With respect to price, I am informed that the basic price of sockeye salmon in Japan, plus freight and 15 per cent duty, plus labelling and selling costs, is so close to the current Canadian market price that there is little or no margin of profit for the Canadian importer.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Patterson) asked a supplementary question in the same regard on Friday last and I said I would answer him fully today. In connection with the question asked on the matter of imported Japanese canned salmon, may I say this.
The matter of using brand labels on canned salmon from Japan was a decision of the companies importing the product. There are no Canadian regulations against the use of such brand labels on imported canned salmon. It would appear obvious that the companies made the decision on the basis that they had spent, over many years, large sums of money

in advertising their brand labels, and being satisfied with the quality of the imported product, not to have used the established labels would have meant the loss of then-advertising and sales promotion campaigns of many years. The practice of using established brand labels on imported canned fish products, where quality is assured, is a common one. The labels mentioned by the hon. member for Fraser Valley are also used on imported canned fish products from other countries, such as shrimps from the United States, sardines from Norway and many other fish imports.
As to the size of the lettering on the labels, "Product of Japan", this condition is governed by section 26 of the Meat and Canned Foods Act. The key words in section 26 are that these words should be printed in a "plain and conspicuous" manner. I might point out for the benefit of hon. members that in the case of meat products there are no specific requirements by the Department of Agriculture with respect to the height or size of labelling on importations of canned meats. In other words, the regulations concerning country of origin are identical for canned fish products and canned meat products.
As far as the labelling of imported Japanese canned salmon is concerned, I am satisfied that there have been no attempts to deceive the Canadian consumer in so far as tne designation of the country of origin is concerned. In one or two instances where the Department of Fisheries considered the words "Product of Japan" were not sufficiently conspicuous on the label, this condition has been corrected by the importing companies willingly and without delay.
I might add that all the canned salmon imported from Japan has not been brought into Canada by British Columbia canning companies. In quite a number of cases imports have been made by brokers in Montreal and other centres.

subtopic: CONSTRUCTION AND PURCHASE OF BRANCH LINES IN MANITOBA

speakeroldname: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister of Transport) moved
subtopic: CONSTRUCTION AND PURCHASE OF BRANCH LINES IN MANITOBA
speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to authorize and to provide for the construction by Canadian National Railway Company of a line of railway from Optic lake to Chisel lake in the province of Manitoba, being approximately fifty-two miles, at a total estimated expenditure of $8,840,000, not to be exceeded by more than 15 per cent; and also to authorize the purchase from The International Nickel Company of Canada, Limited, by the said railway company, of a line of railway from a point on the Hudson Bay Railway line at or near Sipiwesk to a point on the Burntwood river at or near Mystery lake in the province of Manitoba, a distance of thirty miles, more or less, at a price not exceeding $5,400,000; to authorize the issue by the said railway company of securities that may be guaranteed by Her Majesty in right of Canada to finance the construction and purchase of the said lines; and, in order that the said railway company may forthwith proceed with construction and the purchase of the said lines of railway, to authorize temporary loans to the said railway company out of the consolidated revenue fund upon terms and conditions prescribed by the governor in council and secured by securities of the said railway company.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Courtemanche in the chair.

subtopic: CONSTRUCTION AND PURCHASE OF BRANCH LINES IN MANITOBA
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I intend to
make a short statement at the opening of this debate. First I would ask to have distributed among hon. members some eight copies of a map showing the area in which the railway lines are being built. I have

Canadian National Railways always found it a lot easier to follow what is going on if I could see on a map where the particular projects were being constructed, and I would ask that the maps be distributed amongst hon. members.
This resolution seeks to authorize the Canadian National Railways, first, to construct a line of railway from Optic lake to Chisel lake, in the province of Manitoba, a distance of 52 miles, at an estimated cost of $8,840,000; and second, to purchase and operate as part of the Canadian National Railways system a line of railway being constructed by the International Nickel Company of Canada, Limited, between a point on the Hudson Bay Railway near Sipiwesk and a point on the Burntwood river near Mystery lake, also in the province of Manitoba, a distance of 30 miles, at a price not exceeding $5,400,000.
The main purpose of the proposed railway lines is to provide outlets for the mines which are being developed both at Chisel lake and in the vicinity of Moak and Mystery lakes. In addition, the lines would aid in the development of a substantial area which shows evidence of possessing considerable mineral wealth.
Chisel lake lies about 80 miles northeast of The Pas and 52 miles east of Optic lake, which is a point on the Lynn lake line of the Canadian National Railways. Substantial ore reserves, consisting mainly of zinc and copper, are being developed in the Chisel lake area on the property of the Hudson Bay Mining and Smelting Company, Limited, and rail service to move this ore to the mining company's mill at Flin Flon will be required by 1960.
The Mystery lake branch line would serve principally to move large nickel deposits owned by the International Nickel Company in the vicinity of the townsite of Thompson, and also in the Mystery-Moak lakes area, a short distance to the north. It would also serve the International Nickel processing plant at Thompson, consisting of a mill, a smelter and a refinery, in addition to the townsite itself with a population of 8,000 people. The deposits in the Mystery-Moak lakes area will be linked to Thompson by a private railway owned and operated by the International Nickel Company. The 30-mile railway which the Canadian National proposes to purchase would therefore connect the townsite itself with the Hudson Bay Railway.
The construction of this line has been financed by the International Nickel Company because it was desirous of obtaining railway service at the earliest possible date and the Canadian National Railways did not have the necessary parliamentary authority to make the required capital expenditures. In the circumstances, the management of Canadian

National agreed to let the nickel company build the line with the company's own funds and subject to the authorization of parliament, to purchase the line upon its completion, provided construction was to the entire satisfaction of the railways chief engineer and in accordance with standards of construction approved by the board of transport commissioners.
To guard against excessive costs which might result from the desire of the nickel company to construct the line in a short period of time, it was agreed that the purchase price would be the costs which Canadian National would have incurred if the line had been built by it in the normal course of events and under a normal construction schedule. Limited operations by the Canadian National under a temporary lease arrangement have already begun over this line in order to meet the urgent needs of industry.
I am advised that in both cases the mining developments to which I have referred are of such magnitude that the construction, in one instance, and the purchase, in the other instance, of the proposed branch lines would constitute good business ventures. Nevertheless, the Canadian National has secured from both of the industries concerned guarantees of a minimum volume of traffic or minimum revenues for a period of ten years with adequate penalties should traffic or revenues in any year fall short of the guarantee.
I trust that the resolution will commend itself to the house as an important step towards the development of a substantial area of northern Canada and the opening up of new frontiers. Perhaps the house will permit me to add that when the bill that will follow the resolution has been given second reading I propose to move that it be referred to the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines.

subtopic: CONSTRUCTION AND PURCHASE OF BRANCH LINES IN MANITOBA
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the resolution now before the committee is preliminary, as the minister has indicated, to the introduction of a measure to authorize Canadian National Railways to do two things; first, to construct a line of railway from Optic lake to Chisel lake in the province of Manitoba, a distance of approximately 52 miles, at a total estimated cost of $8,840,000 and, second, to purchase from the International Nickel Company of Canada a line of railway from a point at or near Sipiwesk on the Hudson Bay Railway to a point on the Burntwood river at or near Mystery lake in the province of Manitoba, a distance of 30 miles, at a price not exceeding $5,400,000.
I should like to mention to the committee that as favourable consideration was given

to both of these projects by the former government of which I was a member I may assure the committee that it is not our intention to delay the passing of the resolution or the measure which will follow the adoption of the resolution. I think, however, that the presentation of this resolution does afford an appropriate occasion to emphasize the importance of railroad development to the economy of Canada.
I do not want to spend much time in dealing with this aspect of the question but I do think it is fair to point out that railroad building in Canada came to a virtual halt many years ago. We had some 42,047 miles of railway in operation in 1930, 42,248 miles in 1948 and 42,953 in 1952. The difference between the last two figures which I have just given is explained by the inclusion in the statistics for the first time of the 705 miles of railway in Newfoundland which were taken over in 1949. But I should like to emphasize that since 1952 a number of important projects have been carried out, a large part by the Canadian National Railways and some by other railway companies.
I may mention by way of illustration the 144 miles of line from Sherridon to Lynn lake in Manitoba which, of course, makes possible now the construction of the proposed branch line from Optic lake to Chisel lake. I might mention also the 300 mile line partially completed between Beattyville-Chibou-gamau and St. Felicien in the lake St. John area in Quebec, and also the shorter lines from Terrace to Kitimat in British Columbia, from Hillsport to lake Manitouwadge in northern Ontario and more recently the line fom Bartibog to the Tomogonops river in New Brunswick. In addition to these, there are two other important projects, first, that of the Quebec, North Shore and Labrador Railway, a line about 300 miles in length from Seven Islands to Knob lake, and the more recent project of the Pacific Great Eastern 256 miles in length from Prince George, British Columbia, to Dawson Creek.
What is particularly gratifying, I think, to all Canadians in considering the railroad development that has taken place in relatively recent times is that the purpose has been to promote the further development of our natural resources. In some instances it has been the development of iron ore; in other cases, the development of deposits of base metals; in other cases it has been the development of timber resources and, as many hon. members know, in the case of the line between Terrace and Kitimat it has been the development of hydroelectric power for the production of aluminum from imported bauxite.
Canadian National Railways
It is rather significant, Mr. Chairman, that this same pattern is being followed in the case of the two branch lines which are covered by this resolution. I am not familiar with the development expenditures which the Hudson Bay Mining and Smelting Company proposes to make in connection with the zinc and copper deposits to which the minister referred in his explanation a moment ago, but it is a matter of public knowledge that the International Nickel Company last year, before the actual commencement of the Sipiwesk-Mystery lake branch line had been undertaken, announced its intention to spend $175 million for the development of these mineral deposits.
So that, Mr. Chairman, the matter of satisfaction to Canadians is, it seems to me, that railroad development marches forward hand in hand with the development of our natural resources and not only makes possible the development of those resources but also makes it reasonable and good business for the owners or operators of these mineral deposits to lay out very substantial sums for development purposes.
Another matter that I think is of importance and also a source of satisfaction to those who have been interested in transportation in Canada is that in all of the cases of branch lines to which I have referred-there may be other examples which might be cited also-except the Beattyville-Chibougamau-St. Felicien branch line, the traffic in prospect has been sufficient to make the project selfsupporting either immediately or in the shortterm future and it has not been necessary for the government to provide substantial subsidies to make possible the building of these various branch lines. The exception, of course, is the Beattyville-Chibougamau-St. Felicien branch line for which a subsidy of $25,000 per mile was granted by the government because it believed that the construction of that line, which was self-liquidating in part, would open to development a large area of mining territory which ultimately would prove advantageous to the Canadian people. The other exception which I perhaps should mention is the offer of a subsidy which was made in connection with part of the P.G.E. in British Columbia but that is not, of course, connected with the resolution now under consideration.
From what the minister has said in introducing the resolution it is quite clear that this same characteristic, that is to say, of there being adequate traffic to support the project, applies to the two branch lines which are provided for in the resolution now before the committee. In other words, the Canadian

Canadian National Railways National Railways are to lay out rather substantial sums to provide for the capital cost but the revenues, or perhaps I should say additions to the operating profit, which will be in prospect will be sufficient to meet the annual cost of operation and to provide a reasonable return on the company's investment.
As the minister has pointed out, arrangements have been made with regard to future traffic over the branch lines which have been completed by Canadian National Railways with the mining interests that are to be served by these lines. I take it, Mr. Chairman, since the minister has said the bill will be referred, after second reading, to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, that we shall have an opportunity then of going more fully into the traffic arrangements that have been concluded between these two mining companies and the management of Canadian National Railways. Consequently I do not think any useful purpose would be served by my making now any more extensive remarks with regard to those traffic arrangements.
There is only one point which I should like to draw to the attention of the minister particularly, and that is the purchase price of the line to be acquired from the International Nickel Company. During the course of his remarks, he gave the impression that one reason why this particular branch line had not been completed by Canadian National Railways was that the company did not have the necessary parliamentary authority to make the expenditures that would have been needed for that purpose. This is not my own recollection of the circumstances, Mr. Chairman. As I understood the circumstances earlier this year they were that the International Nickel desired to have this branch line completed at a much earlier date than would have been possible had Canadian National proceeded to build it with railway forces or by contractors in the usual manner and by saying "in the usual manner" I mean that no additional expense would have been incurred by the railway in order to hurry the completion of the line before what might be described as a normal date.
When the matter was discussed with me earlier this year, it was represented to me that this was, in the view of the nickel company, a crash program that had to be undertaken, and as I understood the arrangement between the Canadian National and the company it was to the effect that the railway company would pay the nickel company the cost that would have been incurred by Canadian National if the construction of the branch line had been carried out at a normal
[Mr. Marler.l
pace and in the fashion in which such branch lines are usually constructed. I have a record of the cost figure which was considered at the time to be the maximum amount which the railway would be called upon to pay to the nickel company. As I would say to the minister, and he will have the necessary information available in his files, that the cost as set forth in the resolution substantially exceeds the figure which was mentioned at the time the matter came under consideration under the former government.
I do not raise that point as an objection, Mr. Chairman, because I realize fully that the figure we had in mind earlier this year was an estimate, and an estimate made at a time when the work had not been completed and when all the physical difficulties, the delays and the costs had not been definitely established. I should like to suggest to the minister that when the bill is considered in the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, arrangements be made to explain why there has been, over this relatively short period, such a substantial increase in the estimated cost of this branch line. I have no doubt, because of my own experience and association with the management of Canadian National Railways, that the management will be able to give convincing reasons why there is a difference between the two figures. But I do think I should emphasize the matter as it does seem to me that an explanation would be desirable, and I am sure it will be freely given.
I conclude by saying I do not wish for a moment to delay the passage of this resolution, and that it is our intention, for the reasons I have already given, to support not only the resolution but the legislation which is based on it.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: CONSTRUCTION AND PURCHASE OF BRANCH LINES IN MANITOBA
speechtext:
We
in this group are pleased to give our general support to this resolution, and we welcome the statement of the minister that the bill, after second reading, will be referred to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines. I should say that I am happy, not only to indicate the general support of this group for this legislation, but since I am the first member from Manitoba to speak since the matter has been raised I may say that in Manitoba we welcome whole-heartedly these developments that are taking place in the northern part of our province.
We in this group, of course, are anxious that the benefits from these developments might accrue to the people of this country. We are anxious also that, in view of the important part played by the railways in making these developments possible, the

workers who run the railways might get the best possible wages and working conditions as a result of their employment on the railway lines of this country. With these general comments, as I say, we are pleased to give our support to this legislation and to learn that the bill will be referred to the standing committee.
With regard to the last point that was raised by the former minister of transport, the hon. member for St. Antoine-Westmount, it seems to me that the discrepancy between the original estimate of what the Canadian National Railways would have to pay for the Mystery lake-Sipiwesk line and the amount of $5,400,000 which is set out in this legislation should be explained today rather than waiting until this legislation is before the standing committee. The Minister of Transport can speak as often as he likes now that we are in committee on this resolution, and I would hope that he would tell us what he knows with reference to the matter that has been raised by the hon. member for St. Antoine-Westmount. I noted that the last speaker did not give the amount of the estimate made earlier this year. Certainly if the difference between that estimate and this figure of $5,400,000 is of any size, I would say we are entitled to an explanation today rather than having to wait until a later time.
The hon. member for St. Antoine-Westmount will not mind if I take a moment to correct him on his geography. After all, coming from the city of Montreal as he does, he may not be acquainted with the wilds of northern Manitoba. I did note that he referred to the construction not long ago of the branch line from Sherridon to Lynn lake. I heard him say that it was the construction of that line that now made it possible to build the branch line from Chisel lake to Optic lake. Perhaps if the hon. member will look at the map, he will realize that Optic lake is on the part of the line between Cranberry Portage and Sherridon, which has been there for many years.

speechtext: I stand corrected, Mr. Chairman.

subtopic: CONSTRUCTION AND PURCHASE OF BRANCH LINES IN MANITOBA
speechtext: am sure the hon. member would like to have that correction made in so far as the geography of northern Manitoba is concerned. As we have indicated, Mr. Chairman, we welcome the fact that this legislation will be referred to the standing committee and on that basis we are happy to give it our general support.

speechtext:
I should like to say that we in this group will go along with the second reading on the understanding
Canadian National Railways which the minister gave that the bill will be referred to the committee where we can have a more thorough study of it. From just looking over the map here it seems to me that the price may be rather high per mile of construction. Of course, that is information that we cannot get at the moment.
I hope we shall be able to get that information when the bill is before the committee.
Then there is the question of the other smaller line of 33 miles, I think from Mystery lake to Sipiwesk and whether or not the price that the Canadian National Railway Company is going to pay for it would include the rolling stock. Those are all questions that have a bearing on the judgment we shall be able to use when we come into the committee to decide whether or not we shall go along with the proposition as outlined here in the resolution.
Generally speaking, Mr. Chairman, we in this group do not want to delay anything that would lend progress to the development of any part of Canada. It seems to me that the construction of these two lines could add to the development in those areas. If that is so and if the cost is reasonable, I am sure that, all other things considered, we would have no objection to giving our consent to this bill provided, of course, that the information we get in the committee leads us to believe that this is an essential service and that the price is in accordance with ordinary business standards.
Having said that, I think I will leave any further remarks I have to make until we come to the committee stage. Through experience I have found that to be the proper place in which to get the information you desire; and in most cases, when a proposition like this is explained to the committee, I have found that the committee has always been reasonable in granting permission and allowing the construction of such things to proceed.

subtopic: CONSTRUCTION AND PURCHASE OF BRANCH LINES IN MANITOBA
speechtext:
In rising to speak on this bill that is now before us, I would point out that it is one which includes two distinct measures. It provides for the construction of a rail line between a point called Optic lake on the Cranberry Portage-Lynn lake line on the C.N.R. to Chisel lake in the province of Manitoba and for the purchase from the International Nickel Company of Canada of a line from Sipiwesk on the Hudson bay line to a point near Mystery lake, the new townsite of Thompson. From experience in that area I should like to say that those are two measures that should receive the hearty support of this house.
Hon. members from all parts of this house have shown of late great concern, and rightly

Canadian National Railways so, as to what government action should be taken with regard to making possible the continuation of various developments closely related to the base metal mining industry in various parts of Canada. It has been quite evident that their concern has been in relation to the employment or unemployment situation, and in this regard I heartily concur. I might say that in both of the cases we are presently considering we have before us a concrete example as to how we can not only assure continued employment for a great number of people over an expected long period of time but can also open the way for untold hundreds to join the ranks of the permanently employed.

Mr. Speaker, this bill is to authorize the Canadian National, first to construct a 52-mile line of railway, referred to in the bill as branch line No. 1, from Optic lake easterly to Chisel lake at a cost not exceeding $8,840,000 and second, to purchase from the International Nickel Company of Canada a 30-mile line of railway, referred to as branch line No. 2, between Sipiwesk, on the Hudson Bay railway, and a point on the Burntwood river, in the Mystery and Moak lakes area, at a price not to exceed $5,400,000.
With regard to branch line No. 1, substantial ore reserves consisting mainly of zinc and copper, are being developed by the Hudson Bay Mining and Smelting Company in the Chisel lake area. Rail service to move this ore to the mining company's mill at Flin Flon will be required by July 1, 1960. The bill provides for the completion of the line by November 1, 1959, or such later date as the governor in council may approve.
Chisel lake lies about 30 miles north of the Hudson Bay railway and is therefore closer thereto than to the Lynn lake line. However, if a branch line were built from the Hudson Bay railway the distance to be covered to Flin Flon, to which point the ore will be moving, would be 195 miles, whereas, under the present plan, the distance from Chisel lake to Flin Flon will be about 100 miles. The line is to serve primarily the Hudson Bay Mining and Smelting Company, but it will also aid in the development of a substantial area which shows evidence of possessing considerable mineral wealth.
The Canadian National has secured a guarantee of a minimum volume of traffic, under which the mining company has undertaken to ship not less than 350,000 tons of raw ore or in the alternative 70,000 tons of concentrates per annum for a period of ten years. The mining company will pay a penalty on a tonnage basis if shipments in any year fall short of the guaranteed annual tonnage. Any surplus over the guaranteed tonnage accruing in succeeding years would lead to an appropriate refund of penalty by the railway. If, at the end of the ten-year period, an accumulated shortage exists below a total figure of 3,500,000 tons of ore, or 700,000 tons of concentrates, a further period of five years will afford an opportunity for the mining company to recoup the penalties paid. If in any year of this five-year period the mining company ships ore or concentrates in excess of the annual guaranteed tonnage, the railway company will make refunds to the mining

company on a tonnage basis to the extent of such excess, but the total of such refunds is not to exceed the total amount of penalties paid by the mining company.
Branch line No. 2 has been constructed and is being completed as a private project of the nickel company. This was done because of the desire of the nickel company to have rail service available as quickly as possible and, therefore, in advance of the time when parliamentary approval for the construction of the line by the Canadian National could be secured. The nickel company indicated that it would likely take special measures to expedite construction, which would add to the cost of the line. In agreeing to purchase the line, the management of Canadian National made such agreement subject to the condition that the price to be paid to the nickel company would be the costs which the Canadian National would have incurred if the line had been constructed by it in the normal course of events and under a normal construction schedule.
The line will serve principally the new mining developments of the nickel company in the vicinity of the townsite of Thompson and the Mystery-Moak lakes area. These consist of large nickel deposits. The line would also serve the International Nickel processing plant at Thompson, consisting of a mill, a smelter and a refinery, in addition to the townsite itself with a population of
8,000	people. The site of the deposits in the Mystery-Moak lakes area will be linked to Thompson by a private railway owned and operated by the nickel company.
It is expected that the traffic that will result from the establishment of these mines will give the Canadian National earnings sufficient to warrant its purchasing line. There has nevertheless been included in the agreement between the railway and the nickel company a traffic guarantee clause. Under this traffic guarantee, the nickel company has undertaken that the gross tolls received from the traffic to, from and over the branch line will equal in annual value one-tenth of the purchase price of the line in each year for a period of ten years. The agreement provides that if the gross tolls do not meet this guarantee, the nickel company will provide 20 per cent of the difference to the railway company. If, at the end of the ten-year period, the nickel company has paid to the railway company any money under the traffic guarantee clause, the nickel company has a period of five years to recoup the money so paid. During this period of five years, the nickel company will not be under any obligation to the railway company respecting a traffic guarantee, but if in any year for a period of
Canadian National Railways five years the gross tolls received by the railway company exceed in amount one-tenth of the cost of the line the railway company will make refunds to the nickel company to the extent of 20 per cent on each such excess. Refunds to be made by the nickel company to the railway company, if any, during the five-year period are not to exceed the amount of any deficiencies paid to the railway company by the nickel company during the ten-year period to which reference has been made.
The line was sufficiently constructed in October, 1957, to be ready for operation and the nickel company requested that the railway inaugurate service immediately. A temporary lease arrangement was therefore made between the Canadian National and the nickel company under which the Canadian National undertook to operate the line at a rental equivalent to 4J per cent interest on the capital sum invested by the nickel company in the construction of the line under a normal construction schedule. This arrangement was approved by the order in council P.C.1957-1356, dated October 9, 1957, and was subject to the issue of an order of the board of transport commissioners under section 279 of the Railway Act for opening the railway for traffic. Such an order was issued on October 17, 1957, and a spike-driving ceremony took place on Sunday, October 20. The line has since been operated by Canadian National under the lease arrangement just referred to.
As I indicated when the resolution was before the house, it is my intention when the bill has been given second reading to move that it be referred for consideration to the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines.

Besides, he must realize that he is the political leader of a bilingual country comprising the two racial elements with equal rights. Was it not one of the members of his cabinet, namely the Solicitor General (Mr. Balcer) who, on August 16 last, stated in Edmonton-and I am quoting from the newspaper Le Devoir of August 17, 1957-as follows:
We are not just a minority but, in reality, English speaking and French speaking Canadians are here as partners.
In my opinion, it is reasonable that partners be treated with equality and I have no doubt that the Solicitor General will endeavour to bring all his colleagues from the ten provinces to support my bill.
Need I add that there are precedents justifying the adoption of this bill? There are bilingual currency and postal stamps. I do not think that these two first steps to foster good understanding between the two great races of this country have caused any disturbance in Canada or any wrong to a single Canadian citizen. Why would it be otherwise with the measure I am proposing today?

Mr. Speaker, having seconded my good friend from Beauce (Mr. Poulin), I am pleased to say a few words in support of this proposed legislation.
This is the third time that the bill on bilingual cheques, introduced by my hon. friend from Beauce has been submitted to the approval of the house. While the adoption of such a measure would prejudice no one in this country, it would be an act of justice towards one third of its people, whose language is French, it would help strengthen national unity, and would favour better understanding between the two great races in Canada.
By reason of our geographic situation, we are forced to absorb, willy-nilly, the American way of life as pictured to us by TV, the radio, newspapers, tourists, and by business carried on in the language of two thirds of the people of Canada.
May I say, Mr. Speaker, that the traditions, the religion and the language of the French-Canadian people of this country constitute obstacles to American assimilation which, by the very nature of things, would otherwise be quite unavoidable.
The adoption of my hon. friend's bill would be a further step towards unity between two great races that make Canada a great and unique country, and, at the same time, it would be a guarantee of survival.
The recognized equality of the two great races would seem to demand the adoption of such a measure, and I hope that all hon. members from both sides of the house will make it a point of honour to see that, from now on, all cheques issued by the government, anywhere in Canada, be printed in the two official languages.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in considering this resolution, two points strike my attention. First, what is its objective and how can it be reached?
The first and main objective, in the minds of the hon. members of the house, is and should be complete national unity. Now I honestly believe that the best way to reach that goal is to follow the dictates of plain common sense.

All racial or religious differences which I have observed in this country, or anywhere in the world, are due to two causes. First, they are often prompted and exploited by unscrupulous politicians, or other scoundrels, for their personal benefit or gain; secondly, they may be the by-products of ignorance, lack of understanding or intolerance.
It is so easy, after all, for people to believe the slanders and calumnies about others whom they do not know. That is why, unfortunately, some people take advantage of that human failing to spread suspicions which, in some cases, have proved ineradicable.
I remember that, as a youth, when I was living in the county of Compton, province of Quebec, just two miles from our English village of Gold, there was a French village by the name of Sainte-Marguerite de Lin-wick. At that time there was no kind of social contact or fraternization between us. The Blains, the Lapointes or the Rousseaus gathered around the wood-stove in the general store of Sainte-Marguerite and talked about the Scotch, while the MacCaskills, the MacKays, or the Morrisons were doing likewise at Gould, about the Frenchies. But let some disaster happen, as when fire destroyed Joseph Blain's barn together with all his crops and livestock, or when a cyclone flattened the house of Murdo McLeod, then everybody, French or English, turned up at the bee and pitched in not only in rebuilding destroyed property but in donating a cow, a pig, a load of hay, or furniture. When the bee was finished,-always climaxed by a dance-not only were the buildings up again but they were well furnished.
How amazing it was to sense that surge of friendship spreading from village to village for a few months, everyone realizing that people he had looked down upon until then were, after all, no worse than himself, nor different!
But, alas, in less than six months, the old situation emerged again, until some new disaster again revived the fellow-feeling.
Was that not in itself a tragedy, this situation where fundamentally kind-hearted and generous people failed to appreciate one another or to get together except when visited by some calamity.
It strikingly shows the magnitude and importance of the task facing us if we really want to promote understanding and mutual respect among all the Canadians scattered throughout our great and wonderful country.
Another example which comes to my mind happened in 1942 when I had the privilege of serving in a French-Canadian regiment, the St. Lawrence Fusiliers. Only six of us in the whole unit could speak English and yet never,

in all my five years in the army, was I made to feel so welcome, nor was I so well treated, as during those three months I passed with French-speaking comrades.
As I said at the outset, it is easy to accept as the truth the gossip we hear about people we do not know, but once we have learned to know one another, we realize that those seeds of discord are sown in the mind of Canadians for the sole purpose of creating disunity, by greedy opportunists who have no other concern but their own advantage and profit.
In fact, Canada is made up not only of two but of many nationalities, each of which contributes to our national culture and heritage. However, Canada recognizes two official languages, those of the two main groups which make up its population. This must be understood if we wish to work together toward national unity, remembering that privileges granted to one group can in no way detract from the prerogatives enjoyed by the others.

speakeroldname: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister of Transport) moved
maintopic: LEGISLATION TO AUTHORIZE LOANS FOR ADDITIONAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a bill to authorize the Minister of Finance to make loans to the Hamilton harbour commissioners, out of the consolidated revenue fund, not exceeding in the aggregate $4 million for the purpose of constructing additional dockage and other facilities in the harbour.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Rea in the chair.

maintopic: LEGISLATION TO AUTHORIZE LOANS FOR ADDITIONAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this resolution seeks to authorize a loan of $4 million to the Hamilton harbour commissioners to permit them to participate in an $8 million harbour development program to be completed in 1960. The trade to Hamilton harbour, both foreign and domestic, has been steadily increasing in recent years. The established industries have definite plans for expansion; other industries are moving to Hamilton and the recent announcement of the Ontario hydro of the construction of a system of a steam generating plant all add materially to the rate of increase of waterborne traffic. The completion of the St. Lawrence seaway will, I am sure, greatly contribute towards this rate of increase.
The Hamilton harbour commissioners propose to construct a new transit shed on the Wellington street terminal, now being extended by the Department of Public Works. They propose to create by 1959 a new terminal slip at Ship street and to construct for 1960 a new slip at Strathearne street. The Wellington street transit shed will cost the commissioners $1 million and the new slips at Ship street and Strathearne street are estimated to cost $3 million each, the commissioners to pay one-half of this cost and the remainder to be borne by the Department of Public Works. In addition, the Department of Public Works would carry out a large dredging program costing $1 million in connection with the Strathearne street slip.

Hamilton Harbour Commissioners
A loan at the rate of 4-J- per cent for a term of 40 years is proposed, and on this basis the annual financing for the Wellington street transit shed would be $50,000 and for the Ship street and Strathearne street terminals $75,000 each, making a total of $200,000 annually. An examination of the harbour commissioners financial position indicates that the expected revenues above expenditures would be well in excess of $200,000 per annum and that under normal circumstances the commissioners would have no difficulty in meeting their commitments.
These projects were examined by the departments of public works and finance and my department on the spot some months ago, and after further discussion in Ottawa it was agreed that this expansion program in Hamilton merits support. I trust that the resolution will commend itself to the house as an important step to facilitate the development of Hamilton harbour and to permit the Hamilton harbour commissioners to keep in step with the demands of waterborne traffic being made upon them. I might say that when the bill is before the house I intend to move that it be referred to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines.

maintopic: LEGISLATION TO AUTHORIZE LOANS FOR ADDITIONAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as the minister has pointed out, this resolution is a necessary prerequisite to the introduction of a bill which will enable the government to lend to the Hamilton harbour commissioners an amount not exceeding $4 million for the purpose of constructing additional dockage and other facilities in Hamilton harbour. I think that in considering the resolution it must be remembered that the Hamilton harbour commissioners are a separate and autonomous corporate body and that this is not one of the national harbours which falls under the jurisdiction of the national harbours board. Consequently, in considering the terms of the resolution it must be borne in mind that there is a distinction to be made between these autonomous harbour commissions and the national harbours board itself which is an agency of the crown and at the same time a national institution.
Of course, I am fully aware that in the past the federal government has followed the practice of advancing the capital sums required for harbour dredging in the harbours which, having harbour commissioners, still do not fall under the jurisdiction of the national harbours board. But I think that this is the first case which has come to my notice in which the rather extensive program referred to somewhat briefly by the minister is to be carried out as a joint operation by

the public works department of this government and by the local harbour commission itself. Perhaps I might come back to that point in a moment.
I should like to say, considering the matter more in a general way, that it was my experience when I was minister of transport that a decision had been pretty well reached that advances made to autonomous harbour commissioners for harbour improvements from time to time would be made on the basis that the investment would be self-liquidating.
I think that was a sensible policy to follow because naturally when the government came to consider the propriety of making an advance or of the making of an expenditure which it would itself support, all of the pertinent facts would be taken into account so that, so far as it is possible in advance to predict what the future development of a harbour will be, consideration would be given to all the pertinent factors in order that an estimate might be reached of the additions to the revenues of the harbour and at the same time the additions to operating expenses and particularly, when advances of this kind were considered, the addition of the burden of interest and amortization of principal.
I think that such a policy has much to commend it because otherwise harbour commissioners who are inspired by a natural and understandable wish to possess more attractive and perhaps more modern facilities might very easily be tempted to borrow substantial sums from the government in the expectation that by the expenditure of the moneys in question business would be attracted to their harbours and that, in their estimation at least, revenues in sufficient amount would be developed to enable the harbour commission to repay the moneys so borrowed. But clearly if this were done widely and without the element of-I would not like to use the word "supervision"-the economics of the projects being given careful attention, developments of this kind would give rise to a state of affairs which I think in the long run could only be disadvantageous to local harbour commissioners and of course to the government itself if the government were financing such improvements. Consequently, when I was associated with the Department of Transport it was felt it would be desirable to have the fullest economic study made of projects of this kind in order to determine to what extent the proposed capital expenditures were justified.
It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, we have quite an unusual situation here. It is common knowledge, I think, that the Department of Public Works has, for example in the case of the Toronto harbour commission, carried out

extensive dredging projects at the expense of the federal government so as to provide deep water navigation up to the facilities which have been constructed by the Toronto harbour commission itself. I can, however, recall no instance in which the government has used public funds, obviously through the budget of the Department of Public Works, and either alone or jointly with any harbour commission undertaken the construction of facilities which by their very nature are revenue producing.
The facts as given by the minister should, I think, remove any particular disquiet as to the security of the $4 million which is to be advanced by the government, and which it is necessary that the committee should consider when adopting this particular resolution. But I think the government should perhaps consider what will be the effect of the policy which it seems now to be inaugurating in placing under the control of separate and autonomous harbour commissions valuable facilities producing revenue, when the revenues from those facilities will be used exclusively for the purposes of the harbour commission.
Of course, I have no knowledge whatever of the cost of these facilities other than the information which the minister has just given. It is not possible for me, with the rather limited information at my disposal, to know how useful the facilities which the minister has described will be; what are likely to be the revenues which they will produce when fully developed and, let us say, fully used. I do believe the government owes it to the committee to explain the reasons which have led them to depart from past policies in this connection, and to say whether in other places in Canada where additional harbour facilities are going to be required they will follow the precedent which appears now to be established of bearing jointly with the harbour commission the cost of the improvement it may be thought suitable to make to the local harbour. I think there is a very real and obvious distinction to be made between expenditures made in the national harbours and those made in the case of autonomous bodies such as Hamilton, Toronto, New Westminster and a few others. I think the minister should explain what are the reasons which have led the government to depart from the more or less established policies.
Coming back to the national harbours, I would say that it is quite obvious where improvements are made by the national harbours board it is quite proper that they should be financed by the government. If the facilities produce more revenue than is needed, in other words more revenue than 96698-1141
Hamilton Harbour Commissioners is required to repay the interest and amortization of the investment, the excess will accrue to the national harbours board and will find its way into the accounts of the government at the end of each year. But in this particular case the revenue which will accrue from the improvements to which the minister has referred will accrue to the commission itself. I do not reject the idea, I am just questioning the advisability of embarking on a policy in which the cost of revenue producing improvements is borne jointly by the federal government and the commission itself.
At all events the minister will perhaps deal with that question before the resolution is adopted. He has referred, of course, to the question of the traffic in Hamilton harbour. I think it is gratifying to note that there has been, as the minister has said, an increase both in foreign and domestic traffic. As I recall, about a year or so ago when I had occasion to examine the volume of overseas traffic which was then passing through the canal system I observed that of the not very large proportion which originated from or was destined to Canadian ports on the great lakes, the portion going to Hamilton represented a fairly substantial percentage. I do not recall the exact figure but my impression is that more than two-thirds of the total overseas traffic was destined to or originated from the two ports of Toronto and Hamilton.
The minister has referred also to the probable building at Hamilton of a thermal plant by the hydro electric commission of Ontario. Quite obviously, that should provide additional traffic for Hamilton harbour. So far as the St. Lawrence seaway is concerned, I think we all believe there is going to be an expansion in overseas traffic, although while I was minister of transport no one in the department seemed anxious to put down on paper any very positive estimate as to the exact amount of that traffic. In any event, as I understand what the minister has said, it is the belief of his department that the increase in foreign and domestic traffic, the traffic that is likely to be generated by the establishment of a thermal plant at Hamilton, and the additional traffic which may be expected to develop when the seaway is finished will, all in all, justify the new facilities and provide revenues adequate to meet at least the interest and amortization of the $4 million covered by this resolution.
I should like, Mr. Chairman, to hear what the minister has to say with regard to the broader question of these facilities being provided at the joint expense of the local

Hamilton Harbour Commissioners harbour commission and the Department of Public Works. I realize, of course, that is not the principal issue in this resolution. The principal issue in this resolution, on which I think there can be no possible disagreement, is that the resolution is a prerequisite to a bill which will authorize the Minister of Finance to lend $4 million to the Hamilton harbour commissioners for the carrying out of this program. From what the minister has said, and bearing in mind the very well-established reputation of the harbour commission itself, its long record of successful and good administration of the harbour, I do not think any of us would have any qualms about approving the resolution. However, I do hope the minister will tell us something about the subsidiary question of the financing of these harbour facilities jointly by the federal government and by the local commission.

During the first year in which I was a member of this house I had the pleasure one week-end of visiting Hamilton as a member of a party of members of the house. While I realize that a brief visit does not qualify me to discuss in any detail the merits of this project, certainly during that visit I gathered enough knowledge of the interest in the affairs of the city taken by Hamiltonians to understand the interest of the Hamilton harbour commission in this particular project.
I was interested in listening to the brief statement made to the house by the Minister of Transport and also in listening to the statement made by the former minister of transport. Perhaps I might be permitted to observe that the statement of the former minister of transport was perhaps a little bit more discursive than were some of the statements he used to make when he was sitting across on the other side of the house on occasions similar to this.

maintopic: LEGISLATION TO AUTHORIZE LOANS FOR ADDITIONAL FACILITIES

I feel that the introduction of the resolution raises one or two questions which I certainly should like to have the Minister of Transport answer for us before the resolution passes. If I understood correctly the remarks of the former minister, he suggested to the house that in this resolution there has been some departure from what has been the former policy of the department. I can believe that perhaps the former minister may have more knowledge of some of the details of this project than he has indicated to us in the house. I do not imagine this project has reached the present stage overnight. The question which

occurs to me, of course, is whether this is the first time an advance of this kind is being made to one of the autonomous harbour commissions and how similar this resolution is to any previous arrangement for financing works by the independent harbour commissions as distinct from works under the national harbours board. I think the Minister of Transport should make it clear to the house whether this is a particular project or a particular policy in respect of the Hamilton harbour commission or whether other autonomous harbour commissions, if they had similar needs and were under similar circumstances, would be able to receive similar consideration.
I have some interest in this matter in view of the fact that one of the autonomous harbour commissions lies within the boundaries of my own constituency. While I have no present indication that they may be approaching the government with any proposals for extension of harbour facilities, nevertheless I think it should be clear to us as members of the house from various parts of the country and with interests in various ports of the country just what the government is doing in bringing forward this proposal. I have no reason to doubt that my colleagues on the railways, canals and telegraph lines committee will be able to give full support to the measure as it reaches further stages, but I feel that one or two of these points which have been mentioned by the former minister of transport as well as the question which I have raised should be answered by the minister while we are discussing this measure at the resolution stage.

maintopic: LEGISLATION TO AUTHORIZE LOANS FOR ADDITIONAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
I do not intend to occupy too much time of the committee because there is no reason why this motion should be held up. After all, I believe it is expedient that the Hamilton harbour commission should extend its facilities in the light of the fact that the St. Lawrence seaway is certainly going to make upon it demands that at the present moment do not exist and are not likely to
come into being as a result of ordinary traffic. [DOT]
I noticed that the hon. member for St. Antoine-Westmount-maybe I misunderstood him-was trying to bring the city of Hamilton into this question of financing this project. Frankly I do not think that is good business. The city of Hamilton or for that matter any other municipality has plenty on its hands under existing economic conditions without entering into the question of extending harbour facilities, particularly when those extensions arise out of the fact that what is going to occur is not because of anything that Hamilton does but because of something for the general benefit of Canada itself. I believe

that this is a matter solely for the Hamilton harbour commissioners and for the board of harbour commissioners here in Ottawa. I think this is an excellent opportunity for the government to show its willingness to assist municipalities or districts, as far as that is concerned, to a reasonable extent to extend their facilities in order to help out national causes.
I am a little bit worried, of course, because I come from Burnaby and we are faced with the fact that we have harbours on the Fraser river. I hope this will be a step in the direction of the federal government showing its willingness to enter into this question broadly across the country and to help out the harbour commissions on the Fraser river. If I could suggest it to the Minister of Transport, one of the first steps they could take in the matter is to try to correlate the activities of the two harbour commissions at present on the Fraser river.
As to this loan to the Hamilton harbour commission, I notice that our friend the hon. member for Comox-Alberni was a little bit worried that it was going to set a precedent. I am not the least little bit worried about their setting a precedent because, as far as I am concerned, they could not set a better precedent in this world than the one they are setting now, if that is what it is going to be, in helping harbour commissions to help Canada into a better position than that in which it is at the present time.

maintopic: LEGISLATION TO AUTHORIZE LOANS FOR ADDITIONAL FACILITIES
speechtext: I should like to ask the minister a question. Is not 40 years a long time over which to spread $4 million? A harbour board is not likely to see 1997 and most of us do not expect to see it. Could it not be 20 years at four per cent, leaving out future generations?

maintopic: LEGISLATION TO AUTHORIZE LOANS FOR ADDITIONAL FACILITIES
speechtext: The answer to that question is that if you try to pay off that loan in 20 years at four per cent, you just do not pay off the loan.

maintopic: LEGISLATION TO AUTHORIZE LOANS FOR ADDITIONAL FACILITIES
speechtext: Thank you.

maintopic: LEGISLATION TO AUTHORIZE LOANS FOR ADDITIONAL FACILITIES
speechtext: I hope the minister is going to outline the question of policy.
