Yes. The hon. member for St. Antoine-Westmount asked with regard to our being willing to advance a loan for half of the total cost of the Hamilton harbour commission while the Department of Public Works is making a considerable investment. In reply I might say to him that we believe that is fair and reasonable assistance to an important harbour in Canada which we believe is growing in order to assist it to develop and grow. The hon. member for St. Antoine-Westmount perhaps feels that this is too generous a bill for the Hamilton
Hamilton Harbour Commissioners harbour commission. I do not know whether or not that is his view but this is what we consider to be a fair proposal and we have submitted it in that spirit. We are satisfied with this proposition and feel it is a good and satisfactory way in which to help a growing city help itself. Now I wonder if the hon. member for Comox-Alberni would repeat his question.

maintopic: LEGISLATION TO AUTHORIZE LOANS FOR ADDITIONAL FACILITIES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the question I asked of the Minister of Transport was whether this was the first time an arrangement of this kind has been entered into by the federal government with one of the autonomous harbour boards and, if it was not, whether he could give us some indication as to what departures, if any, from previous arrangements were being made in this instance? I may say for the benefit of the member for Burnaby-Richmond that I was not expressing any concern over the setting of a precedent but I would like to know the facts.

maintopic: LEGISLATION TO AUTHORIZE LOANS FOR ADDITIONAL FACILITIES
speechtext: Well, Mr. Chairman, I am not really an expert on harbour assistance. I do know however that through the Department of Public Works the government is assisting the Toronto harbour commission in respect of considerable dredging operations in helping the harbour to become prepared for the opening of the St. Lawrence seaway. I also know that at the present time this government is considering what help it might give to both the Department of Public Works and the Department of Transport in an examination of possible assistance to the harbour at the lakehead. I believe it is the duty of government, where it can do so, to assist people to help themselves but I do not think there is any hard and fast rule as to exactly what a government should do in any particular set of circumstances. I believe it is the role of government to assist the communities in respect of development projects which will help their own economy and the economy of the country to grow and, with respect to this plan of action, I feel this government is acting correctly in moving towards the helping of people to develop this growing country of ours.

maintopic: LEGISLATION TO AUTHORIZE LOANS FOR ADDITIONAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
Well, Mr. Chairman, I think perhaps the minister has not really answered my question. I am quite aware of the fact, of course, that through the Department of Public Works quite a large number of harbour development projects are undertaken and money is spent for that purpose in many parts of the country, but the real point of my question was whether or not there had been previous occasions on which an arrangement such as is described in this

Hamilton Harbour Commissioners resolution had been entered into. That is to say where, out of the consolidated revenue fund of Canada money is advanced to one of the autonomous harbour commissions for the undertaking of their capital works projects. Now if the answer is not at the minister's fingertips-and I understand of course that he has not a long background of experience with the detailed activities of the Department of	Transport-perhaps
arrangements could be made to have the answer given in the committee stage of the bill.

maintopic: LEGISLATION TO AUTHORIZE LOANS FOR ADDITIONAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
Well, Mr. Chairman, I know for instance that in the hon. member's own province the Department of Public Works assists an autonomous harbour commission, namely that in New Westminster, and has assisted them considerably in the past with respect to dredging operations. The government has assisted various harbour commissions in various ways, but I do not feel there is any set pattern in which we say we will or will not carry out any particular set of operations. Whenever something appears to be necessary to be done, as I understand it, my department and the Department of Public Works look into the matter to see if it is justified and to see if there is some way in which the government can help the harbour commission to do the job which it wants to do.
Now it seems strange to me that while members usually urge the government to do more, we find tonight that members are urging the government to do less. The government, I think, is doing a reasonable job of assistance to the Hamilton harbour commission in helping itself and in expanding and it seems to me from the remarks made by members of the opposite side of the house there is a certain criticism implied. There seems to be an idea abroad that we are doing a little too much; that perhaps we should be thinking about this a little bit more carefully; that perhaps we should not lend so much; perhaps we should have the loan paid back in 20 years instead of 40 years and perhaps the Department of Public Works should not be participating in the way it is.
Now, if the hon. members opposite feel that way it is certainly different from what usually takes place when measures of this kind come before the house. I am speaking for the government in this matter and I feel that the government is adopting a good, sensible and progressive policy to help the harbour commissions help themselves. If members on the opposite side of the house now feel we are being too generous-and of course they are entitled to their own view- then I am surprised to hear it. If that is


the feeling, as I say, it is quite different from what usually takes place, but of course now we have a new government which looks at things a little differently and perhaps we are going to get a brand new type of criticism.

I wonder if perhaps the hon. member for Trinity-Conception who has just risen to his feet would mind if I pursued this a little further because I think the Minister of Transport has, in his last remarks, entirely misrepresented my reason for rising to ask him questions. I cannot see how he could possibly have read into anything I have said any desire to oppose the proposal which has been put forward. Surely if we rise simply for the purpose of obtaining a little more information from the minister than he saw fit to give us at the opening of the discussion we cannot be considered as opposing the proposal which the government is bringing forward.
Now I thought my question was perfectly simple and straightforward; I did not say one word as to whether I was for this measure or against it except that I did say at the start that I understood and appreciated the desire of the Hamilton harbour commission and the people of that city to have their harbour facilities extended and I fully expected that we would be able to go along with this proposal. Now I said that quite definitely. What I wanted to know was simply whether this was the first time the government had chosen to adopt this particular pattern of providing assistance by the mechanism of a loan which I understood is to be repayable under certain terms and conditions to the consolidated revenue fund.
In my initial remarks I did raise a further question as to whether or not we can understand from the minister that, under the same terms and conditions, if other autonomous harbour boards approached the government with a proposal which stood on its merits in the way the minister indicates this one does, they could expect the same kind of arrangement might be worked out. That is all I wanted to know from the minister. I had no desire to create in his mind that I was in any way opposed to his proposal when I asked these questions.

Well, Mr. Chairman, this bill, as I mentioned earlier, will go before the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines where full questioning will be possible and at whose meetings the officials of my department will be present to answer all questions that can be put. As I explained earlier, I have held this portfolio for only a limited time and I am not an

expert on the past history of these things. I am doing the job at the present time and trying to look to the future.
Regarding looking to the future, I am glad to be able to assure the hon. member for Comox-Alberni that if other harbour commissioners put forward propositions which appear to be as economically sound as this one does, we will be pleased to receive them and to consider them and to look on< them very favourably. Mr. Chairman, it seems to me from what the minister is saying that he is initiating a new policy. I am not against that policy and I am certainly not against spending money for harbour commissions or public works. We find it mighty hard to get from the Minister of Public Works what we require to assist our people in improving their living standards.
But we have a harbour in Newfoundland, St. John's. The minister has seen it himself and I think he will realize that it is an important and growing port. I am given to understand that they need improvements down there, and I am hoping-and the minister has partly answered my question when replying to the last speaker-that if the people in St. John's apply to him under the same conditions as Hamilton has done he will grant the same facilities as he is granting Hamilton. The minister has already said he will consider these schemes on their merits. That leaves an escape. But I think that if he grants this to Hamilton he cannot deny it to anyone else who asks for the same concessions under the same conditions, and I should like an assurance that if the harbour commission in St. John's puts the case up to him, and if they need the improvement, they will get the same terms as Hamilton is getting.

maintopic: LEGISLATION TO AUTHORIZE LOANS FOR ADDITIONAL FACILITIES
speechtext: As I said to the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, I am very glad to assure the hon. member that, if the harbour commission of St. John's brings forward to us a proposition which on examination appears to be as economically sound as this one does and gives an equal good assurance of payment at an economic rate of interest over a reasonable period of time we will be very glad to look at it as favourably as we are looking on this application.

Hamilton Harbour Commissioners
I think the present minister has missed the point of the queries. He drew into the discussion a mention of the lakehead. speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker. The purpose of this bill is to extend the benefits provided by the Canadian Vessel Construction Assistance Act in order to give further encouragement to the construction and conversion of vessels in Canada.
The bill is a rather technical one involving income tax law. As the house leader has already said, when it has had second reading I propose to move that it be referred to the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines.
Before going into the provisions of the bill itself I might summarize the existing provisions of the act by stating that the benefits granted are twofold. The first is the provision of a higher rate of depreciation, not exceeding 33J per cent on a straight line basis, as opposed to the normal rate of 15 per cent on the reducing balance allowed under the Income Tax Act. This special rate of depreciation applies only, of course, to vessels built, converted or altered in Canada. The second benefit is the freedom from recapture of depreciation where the proceeds of sale of a ship are used for replacement in Canada.

The amending bill enlarges and extends the conditions under which the benefits of the act can be obtained. These extensions are necessary because of the fact that shipbuilding in Canada is a more expensive undertaking than it is in European or Japanese yards. In comparison with United Kingdom yards, Canadian shipbuilding costs are about 50 per cent higher. This means that the cost of a ship in Canada is one and a half times that of a similar ship built in the United Kingdom. At the same time we must bear in mind that during the war our shipyards made an immense contribution to the allied cause. There was built up during this period a group of skills the dispersal of which must be prevented. For reasons of national security, these skills would be necessary to us and to our allies in the event of another conflict. For reasons of our national economy as a great trading nation it is also necessary for us to maintain the necessary shipbuilding and ship repairing facilities to meet the needs of the many ships of all nations that come to carry away our exports. The Canadian shipbuilding industry is also an important source of employment for Canadian workmen.
Under the act as it now stands a taxpayer for whom a ship was built in Canada can duly obtain the benefits of a higher depreciation rate while he retains the ship on Canadian registry. In order to assist Canadian shipowners to operate their vessels competitively in the international ocean-going trades we have an arrangement with the United Kingdom whereby Canadian-owned ships may be operated on United Kingdom registry, subject to recall to Canadian registry. These ships will be considered as a Canadian contribution to any allied pool in time of war, and by the nature of the arrangements are subject to Canadian requisition in time of war.
The first amendment extends the benefits of the higher rate of depreciation to the Canadian owner of a ship built or converted in Canada and transferred to a commonwealth registry under conditions satisfactory to the Canadian maritime commission.
This involves a transfer under the special arrangements to which I have referred. Accelerated depreciation is, of course, a form of tax relief. Obviously any form of tax relief is valueless unless the taxpayer is earning sufficient taxable income to take advantage of the relief afforded. The owner cannot earn sufficient income under Canadian registry, but he can do so under United Kingdom registry. Indeed it is a recognized fact that the operation of a 10,000 ton dry cargo vessel on Canadian registry costs $100,000 more per year than it does on United Kingdom registry.
Vessel Construction Assistance
The purpose of this amendment therefore, is to encourage owners building for operation under the transfer arrangements, to build their ships in Canada instead of abroad.
Furthermore, as the act now stands, a taxpayer can obtain the benefit of the higher depreciation rate only if the newly constructed ship is built "by or for" him.
The second amendment involves the deletion of these words "by or for". This will allow Canadian shipyards to build ships, barges or vessels, for later sale to a purchaser not yet identified at the commencement of construction. In other words, it will allow speculative building. As a result, yards will be able to keep their employment cycle more level by undertaking such a venture when there is a slack period. To prevent any undue extension of this benefit, it is restricted to vessels in respect of which no depreciation had been previously allowed to any other taxpayer, either under this act or under the Income Tax Act. Consequently, in practice, the benefit will be available only to the taxpayer who has incurred the additional cost of Canadian building, and it will allow a shipyard to do speculative building with the prospect of being able to attract a purchaser.
The third amendment deals with that part of the act which gives freedom from recapture of depreciation under the Income Tax Act when the vessel is sold, provided the proceeds of sale are used for replacement under conditions satisfactory to the Canadian maritime commission. At present this benefit is available only to the ships sold by the crown in the immediate post-war years or those built since 1949 with the benefits of the act. This amendment makes the benefit of freedom from recapture applicable to the proceeds of sale of any ship regardless of whether or not it was allowed special depreciation or capital cost allowances in the past. This is designed to encourage owners of all classes of vessels to dispose of older equipment and to use the proceeds to build replacements in Canada.
The fourth amendment will allow the Canadian maritime commission to certify that it holds on deposit a sum of money or a guarantee at least equal to the tax payable if satisfactory replacement is not effected, thus allowing the benefits of freedom from recapture of depreciation to be realized during the period between disposition of the old vessel and completion of the new one.
Without this amendment the taxpayer, unless the entire undertaking is completed in one taxation year, is compelled to pay the tax in the year of sale and then to seek reimbursement of the tax in the year when

Vessel Construction Assistance the proceeds of disposition are actually spent for replacement. This obviously makes his financing problems more complicated and more onerous.
The fifth amendment modifies certain income tax practices to ensure that the seller of a ship may enjoy the freedom from recapture at the time the sale is made.
The final amendment provides for the conditions under which any deposit or guarantee may be paid out by the Canadian maritime commission.
As with the other bills I have introduced this evening, Mr. Speaker, when second reading is passed I intend to move that this bill be referred to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines.

Mr. Speaker, if one were to read this bill I think one would have the impression that it is probably the most complex piece of legislation which the house will be asked to consider at this session. But the language is misleading because it contains many technical terms. In fact, however, the objects which it proposes to carry out are fundamentally simple.
I should like to say to members of the house that this Bill No. 72 is drawn in very much the same terms as those of a bill for the same purposes which was introduced at the last session of parliament earlier this year but which, because of time running out, was not disposed of and did not go beyond first reading. In consequence it will be our intention to support the bill now before the house. However, I hope that if critical comments are expressed, the Minister of Transport will not again ask us to vote against the government or to throw it out of office.
Hon. members who had the opportunity of examining the Canadian Vessel Construction Assistance Act will see from its terms that it was adopted obviously in order to encourage the construction of vessels in Canadian shipyards and likewise the carrying out in Canadian shipyards of the work of conversion and major alterations. As hon. members may have gathered from what the hon. minister said in his explanatory remarks, encouragement was given in the form of depreciation at an unusually high rate and of freedom from recapture of depreciation where the proceeds from the sale of a vessel were used for its replacement under conditions satisfactory to the Canadian maritime commission. The provisions concerning depreciation which cover both the case of construction of a vessel in Canada and the case where a vessel has undergone conversion or major alteration in Canada will be found in subsections
[Mr. Hees.l
(1) and (2) of section 3, and the provisions providing freedom from recapture of depreciation will be found in section 4, from which it will be seen that the recapture provisions of the Income Tax Act do not apply where the proceeds are used or the replacement of the vessel is made, as I said a moment ago, under conditions satisfactory to the Canadian maritime commission.
The bill which is before us in effect makes several changes. The first one is to do away with the requirement that the benefits of the act shall accrue only to a taxpayer while a vessel remains on Canadian registry and it will be readily seen from an examination of the bill that one of its purposes is to do away with this requirement as a condition of being entitled to benefits and thereafter to depreciation after the vessel is replaced.
The second provision which it is proposed to change is that it is no longer to be a condition that the vessel in respect of which benefits are allowed shall be built by or for the taxpayer and, as the minister himself pointed out, this has to be done by extending the benefits of the act to vessels built by a shipyard for sale to any purchaser. There is, however, a restriction which has been added in regard to this benefit which did not appear in the bill which I presented at the earlier session this year, and I would hope that when the bill is considered in the standing committee we might have the opportunity of going into this restriction to see whether or not a useful purpose will be served by leaving it in or whether it might be more advantageous to make some other provision with a somewhat similar object in mind.
Quite obviously the taxpayer should not be entitled to depreciate the same vessel twice, but I am not sure that the proviso to which I am referring does not prevent the taxpayer from obtaining full depreciation at the accelerated rate and I am not perfectly certain with respect to the benefits which would otherwise accrue to a taxpayer owning a vessel of the kind qualifying for these benefits, whether that taxpayer should be precluded from passing on the same advantages to someone to whom he might sell that vessel. However, that is rather a technical question and perhaps not at all appropriate to discuss on the second reading of this bill, when of course we are concerned with its principle.
The third change is to extend the operation of subsection (1) of section 4 in the present act, as the minister said, so as to include any vessel whatsoever, instead of limiting its operation to those vessels in respect of which some form of special depreciation or capital cost allowance had been granted in the past.

In that connection I would like to recall what I think was a fairly simple explanation which I gave to the house when the estimates of the Department of Transport were under consideration on August 10, 1956. I would like to quote from what I said on page 7406 of Hansard as follows:
Further modifications will also be brought about in the realm of capital cost allowances. At present, for income tax purposes, it is compulsory to pool vessels that have an exemption from recapture of depreciation, under section 4 of the Canadian Vessel Construction Assistance Act, with other vessels that do not benefit from this exemption. Consequently, when the owner disposes of some or all of the vessels so pooled, his exemption can readily become dependent upon the order in which they are sold. Broadly speaking, if the qualified ships are sold earlier and the unqualified ships later, the sale of the qualified ships may serve to wipe out the undepreciated value of the class. This situation could be remedied by permitting an owner, if he so elects, to treat as a separate prescribed class any vessel or vessels that qualify under section 4 of the act: that is, a vessel the proceeds of sale of which had been used for replacement under conditions satisfactory to the commission.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, in referring to the commission there I was referring to the Canadian maritime commission. I am sure hon. members will agree that the question of whether or not the benefits of the act should or should not accrue, ought not to be dependent upon the order in which the taxpayer disposes of his vessels, and if this is the law it would seem to be an anomaly which ought to be corrected, and that, of course, is the purpose of the third change to which I referred a moment ago.
The fourth change is to allow the Canadian maritime commission, where the replacement of a vessel has not been undertaken but is foreseen, to certify that it holds on deposit or by way of guarantee an amount at least equal to the tax that is paid. This will allow the benefits of the act to be recovered during an interim period instead of requiring payment of the tax and the subsequent reimbursement of it. I think the minister's explanation on this point was perfectly clear that when an owner disposes of his ship the question arises as to whether or not there is to be recapture of the depreciation which he has set up during the time he has owned and operated the vessel, and I think it is desirable that this question could be disposed of finally at that time and the determination not held over until perhaps some much later date when the funds in question are used for the replacement of the vessel, that is to say at the time of the completion of the operation by which the old vessel is replaced by a modern replacement.
As I said earlier, Mr. Speaker, this is legislation which we in this party might well have dealt with earlier this year had the time
Vessel Construction Assistance available been long enough and I do not think, despite the complexity of the language of the bill, it is controversial. Therefore, so far as we are concerned, it is our intention to support the second reading.

Some hon. members may wonder why a member from a central Ontario riding is speaking in support of a bill dealing with the construction of ocean going vessels. In Colling-wood on Georgian bay is one of the finest and most efficient shipyards in all Canada. There are presently employed in those yards between seven and nine hundred highly skilled shipbuilders. That these yards have been able to keep busy with the little governmental aid they have received is indeed a tribute to both the workers and management. In anticipation of the opening of the St. Lawrence seaway, ships are now being built there which will sail both the Atlantic and Pacific coasts of Canada. The passage of this bill means that Canadian shipbuilding will be able to compete with regard to all the shipbuilding needs of Canadian owners wherever ships may be used.
It has not been the policy of the Canadian government to subsidize the building of Canadian merchant shipping, yet in times of need the shipbuilding industry and the shipbuilders are absolutely vital to the security of our country. In Canada we have seen since the end of the second world war many of our great lakes yards virtually disappear. Certainly their work forces are scattered forever. If this bill brings only one ship to the great lakes yards it will be worth while, but I am sure it will mean many new ships for all Canadian shipyards. Without it there is no incentive for Canadian ship owners to build their ships in Canada when the prime cost of ships in foreign yards is as much as 50 per cent less than in Canadian yards.
This act is not a subsidy. It merely permits the owner to write off the cost against earnings at an accelerated rate. As soon as the cost is written off in a minimum of three years the ship will still have many years of earning taxable income for the owners.
This bill ought to commend itself to all hon. members who consider the shipbuilding industry important to our national maturity and to our national security.

The purpose of this legislation, as stated by the minister, is to retain the pool of skills which we have built up, and which we might need in an emergency. speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 169, to amend the Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, although this bill appears to have some formidable provisions in it, its intent is quite simple and it is proposed, if the house is pleased to give the

bill a second reading, to have the measure then referred to the standing committee on banking and commerce where a thorough review can be made of the clauses of the bill and where the superintendent of insurance and any other officials whose presence is desired will be available to discuss the terms in detail.
The policies and practices of Canadian life insurance companies cut deeply across the Canadian economic structure and the welfare of a great multitude of people in Canada. The contracts of life companies are generally made for long terms, involving the future welfare of both policyholders and their dependants. Moreover, most companies have grown enormously during the last decade. Consequently the question of their ownership and control is of serious concern and importance to almost every Canadian.
Life insurance companies are organized either on the mutual basis, without share capital, or on the joint stock basis. Mutual companies are, of course, owned entirely by their policyholders. The great majority of Canadian life companies are joint stock companies but practically all of them issue policies on the participating plan as well as on the non-participating plan. A participating policyholder pays relatively higher premiums but is entitled to participate in the profits of the company from its participating business. As a consequence, the holders of participating policies have a very real interest in the management of the company, an interest going substantially beyond the security of their policies alone. This is recognized in the insurance act by giving participating policyholders the right to attend and vote, either in person or by proxy, at all general meetings of the company and by giving them representation on the board of directors to the extent of at least one-third of the board.
Over the years participating insurance has proved to be the more popular plan in Canada, with the result that most of the life business is transacted on this plan. From this point of view, therefore, it may be said that a well-established life insurance company having a large volume of participating insurance in force, even though organized on the joint stock basis, is to some extent already a mutual company.
The capital stock of a relatively mature life insurance company is usually quite small in comparison with the total funds of the company and its total liabilities. The capital serves a most important purpose in launching a company and in providing protection to the policyholders during the early years. However, as a company grows, the capital
Insurance Companies Act becomes less and less important so far as protection to the policyholders is concerned. This is not to say, of course, that the shareholders are not entitled to the profits resulting from the development of a successful enterprise, or to minimize the value of a proprietary interest in most businesses. In the field of life insurance, both mutual companies and stock companies have their advantages and their disadvantages. Nevertheless, the diminishing role of the capital must be mentioned to point up the fact that the principal strength of a well-established life insurance company lies in the funds accumulated from the premiums paid by its policyholders, especially the participating policyholders, rather than in the capital stock.
From what I have said I think that it can readily be seen that the policyholders' interests in every Canadian life insurance company, whether it be a mutual company or a stock company, are very substantial, and that it may properly be stated that as the companies grow they all tend to become policyholder organizations to an increasing extent.
In recent years a high degree of interest has been displayed in the shares of Canadian stock life insurance companies, and in the case of some companies the price of the shares has risen to levels that scarcely seem justifiable in the light of the dividends being paid and the earnings of the companies. For the most part, our Canadian companies have been built by Canadians with Canadian capital, and the good management and public responsibility shown by the shareholders have been a credit to the industry. Policyholders have been treated fairly and the profits withdrawn by shareholders have not in any case been so large as to suggest that the interests of the policyholders have been affected to their detriment. The companies have at the same time gained an enviable record for reliability. With a new body of shareholders, however, coming into ownership of shares at the very high prices that have been in evidence in recent years it is less certain that past management practices will be continued in every instance.
There has also been great interest manifested in recent years in obtaining control of Canadian life insurance companies, particularly among foreign investors. Prior to 1930, all Canadian life insurance companies were controlled in Canada. About 1930, control of the Montreal Life Insurance Company, head office, Montreal, was acquired by an English insurance company. No other change occurred until 1955 but, since then, control of six Canadian life companies has been acquired

Insurance Companies Act by interests outside of Canada. In 1955 control of the Continental Life Insurance Company, head office, Toronto, was acquired by a Swiss insurance company. In the same year, the Canadian Premier Life Insurance Company, head office, Winnipeg, was incorporated by parliament to take over an existing fraternal benefit society, the Dominion General Benefit Association, and the new company was capitalized entirely by another Swiss insurance company. Early in 1956, control of the Western Life Assurance Company, head office, Hamilton, was acquired by certain United States investors; and later that year, control of the Commercial Life Assurance Company, head office, Toronto, was acquired by Dutch insurance interests. Although most of these companies were quite old, they were relatively small companies.
Early in 1957, control of a much larger company, the Dominion Life Assurance Company, head office, Waterloo, was acquired by a large United States insurance company. More recently still, in June last, control of the Fidelity Life Assurance Company, head office, Regina, was acquired by British insurance interests. I am sure the house is aware of the fact that in at least one other conspicuous case control of the stock of the company nearly passed out of Canadian hands not very long ago.
By reason of the small capital in relation to the aggregate funds of many companies, control of a very large organization may sometimes be obtained through comparatively small outlays in the purchase of shares. These surrounding circumstances, which have been the subject of comments from time to time in the reports of the superintendent of insurance, have led some companies to feel that the best course for their future, including the welfare of their policyholders, would be to purchase their own shares, eventually retiring their entire capital stock and so becoming mutual companies. This course has been followed with outstanding success by some of the largest companies in the United States, notably the Metropolitan Life Insurance Company and the Prudential Insurance Company of America.

maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR CONVERSION OF CAPITAL STOCK COMPANIES INTO MUTUAL COMPANIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Whatever the means may be, it seems desirable that control of Canadian life insurance companies should remain in good hands, and preferably Canadian hands. I am sure that this view is shared by all members of the house. After all, the life insurance business in Canada as represented

by the Canadian life insurance companies is peculiarly a Canadian institution.
The rrfein purpose of this bill is to authorize a procedure whereby a stock life insurance company incorporated by parliament may be converted into a mutual company, if the shareholders and participating policyholders of the company wish to follow this course and if the company is in a financial position to do so. The insurance laws of several of the states of the United States of America include provisions of this kind but our own act has not contained such a provision hitherto.
Under the procedure set forth in the bill, mutualization would be effected through the purchase of its own shares by the company and the cancellation of the shares when all of them have been acquired. Appropriate safeguards have been included to ensure that no company will start on this path unless it has the financial resources to carry the plan through to completion within a reasonable period and to ensure that the shareholders will be treated fairly and the interests of the policyholders will be protected.
Some companies may not wish to mutualize but may, nevertheless, wish to retain their Canadian character in so far as they can. In order to assist them to do so the bill would empower the board of directors of a life insurance company incorporated by parliament to refuse to allow the transfer of shares from Canadian hands to non-Canadian hands. This would be a discretionary power resting with the directors to use or not as they might see fit. However, this power would not apply to enable the directors to prohibit transfers from one non-Canadian shareholder to another. In that respect we are taking nothing away from the rights of any existing shareholder residing outside Canada. In some respects this power is similar to the power already conferred upon the directors by the Insurance Act whereby they may refuse to allow the transfer of any shares that are not fully paid.
The bill would also require that the majority of the entire board of directors of every company incorporated by parliament, whether a mutual company or a stock company, and whether a life insurance company or any other kind of insurance company, must at all times be Canadian citizens resident in Canada. The insurance act now requires that a majority of the directors representing shareholders must be Canadian citizens resident in Canada but no provision is made for mutual companies or as respects the entire boards of companies having policyholders' directors as well as shareholders' directors.
The other point dealt with in the bill relates to fraternal benefit societies. At the

present time, a fraternal benefit society insuring the dependent children of members is required to account for this insurance in a completely separate fund. This requirement was established many years ago at a time when societies were smaller than they are now and generally less experienced in insurance matters, particularly in the insurance of children. Under existing circumstances, there is no longer a need for this requirement and societies have been pressing to have the requirement removed so that they may simplify their accounting methods and also reduce their expenses.
Accordingly, the bill would remove the mandatory requirement that juvenile insurance must be accounted for in a separate fund and would enable fraternal societies to merge the juvenile insurance with similar kinds of adult insurance if they wish to do so. However, societies would still be empowered to maintain a separate fund for juvenile insurance if they so desire.
May I remind the house, Mr. Speaker, that if the house is pleased to give the bill second reading it is the intention to propose that it be then referred to the standing committee on banking and commerce.
